variations.label: Aggressive cut for a hard length constraint
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the target length is a hard platform constraint (an ad character limit, a fixed word count for print) rather than a soft "tighter is better" goal.
variations.prompt:
You are editing the draft below to fit a hard limit of [EXACT CHARACTER OR WORD COUNT] — this is a strict constraint, not a suggestion. Keep it in the exact voice shown in these writing samples:

Voice samples: [PASTE 2-3 SHORT SAMPLES OF THE REAL VOICE]
Draft to edit: [PASTE DRAFT]
Do not change: [e.g. "the core claim," "the CTA wording"]

Cut aggressively if needed to hit the exact limit, prioritizing keeping the single strongest sentence or phrase from the draft intact over preserving everything partially. Confirm the final character/word count at the end.

followUps.label: Still sounds generic — compare against the samples again
followUps.prompt: Compare this edited version line by line against the voice samples I gave you and flag anywhere it now sounds like a competent stranger instead of the same writer. Revise just those lines.

followUps.label: Cut too much of the personality along with the length
followUps.prompt: This cut too much of what made the original distinctive. Restore [SPECIFIC PHRASE OR LINE] and find the length savings somewhere else instead — a redundant sentence or a weak qualifier, not a signature phrase.

followUps.label: One more targeted pass, not a full rewrite
followUps.prompt: This is close, but [SPECIFIC SENTENCE] still reads a little flat. Do one more targeted pass on just that sentence to bring it in line with the voice samples — don't touch anything else in the draft.

followUps.label: Confirm nothing important got cut
followUps.prompt: List everything you removed in this edit, one line each, so I can confirm none of the cuts accidentally removed a fact, claim, or line I needed to keep.

copy-b2-edit-tighten-preserve-voice.walkthrough:
Priya edits copy for a brand with a distinctive, slightly irreverent voice, and her client just sent over a 220-word blog intro that needs to come down to about 140 words before publishing.

Before touching the draft, she pulls two short samples of the brand's actual past writing from an old blog post — sentences with short, punchy openers and a near-total avoidance of exclamation points.

In ChatGPT, she pastes the editing prompt: target word count 140, the two real voice samples, the full 220-word draft, the specific problem ("too long, and repeats the core benefit in both paragraph 1 and paragraph 3"), and what must stay unchanged ("the closing line, word for word — it's already approved").

ChatGPT returns a 145-word edit that removes the redundant second explanation of the same benefit and trims a throat-clearing opening sentence, while keeping the brand's characteristic short declarative sentences and one signature aside intact, and leaving the closing line untouched.

Priya compares it line by line against her two voice samples and notices one paragraph now reads a touch more neutral than the rest. She sends the follow-up: "Compare this against the voice samples and flag anywhere it now sounds like a competent stranger instead of the same writer." ChatGPT flags that exact paragraph and revises it to restore a bit of the brand's characteristic dry humor.

She reads the final version once more against the original samples, confirms the closing line is untouched and the word count is 142, and sends it back to the client. Total time: about 10 minutes.

placeholders.name: ONE PLAIN SENTENCE — THE ACTUAL BENEFIT OR CLAIM
placeholders.what: The real, specific benefit or claim your headlines need to communicate, stated plainly — not a vague theme. A good value is concrete enough to build a headline from directly ("saves 6 hours a week"); a bad one is an abstract idea like "we help businesses grow" that could describe almost anything.
examples: This budgeting app finds an average of $200/month in unused subscriptions.
Our onboarding checklist tool cuts new-hire ramp time from 3 weeks to 5 days.
This course gets beginners writing working code in their first session, not week three.

placeholders.name: X
placeholders.what: This is the Audience field — who these headlines need to speak to. Be specific about who's reading, since a headline that lands for a beginner reads flat to an expert, and vice versa.
examples: freelancers who track expenses across multiple clients
HR managers at companies with 50-200 employees
complete beginners who've never written a line of code

placeholders.name: e.g. blog title, email subject line, ad headline — specify length limit if relevant
placeholders.what: What format the headline is for, plus any length constraint that format enforces (an email subject line has a much tighter effective limit than a blog title). This changes what a "good" headline even looks like.
examples: email subject line, under 50 characters so it doesn't truncate on mobile
blog post title, no strict limit but should stay skimmable, under 12 words
Google search ad headline, hard limit of 30 characters

placeholders.name: PASTE ANY REAL FACTS/NUMBERS AVAILABLE
placeholders.what: Any real, specific numbers or facts you actually have and can back up — used to keep the number-led headline formula honest instead of letting the model invent a bigger, more impressive-sounding stat.
examples: Average savings found per user: $200/month, based on our own product data from the last 6 months.
4-day average onboarding time across our current customer base of 40 companies.
No hard numbers available yet — first cohort just finished, informal feedback only.

variations.label: Single-format focused version (just email subject lines)
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you only need one specific format, not a mixed 5-formula sweep — useful for a quick A/B test setup on a single email send.
variations.prompt:
You are a headline specialist. The core message is: [ONE PLAIN SENTENCE — THE ACTUAL BENEFIT OR CLAIM]. Audience: [X].

Generate 8 email subject line options, 2 each from these 4 formulas: (1) benefit-led, (2) curiosity-led (no clickbait), (3) number/specificity-led (use only real numbers: [PASTE ANY REAL FACTS/NUMBERS AVAILABLE]), (4) direct-address. Each under 50 characters. Score each 1-5 on clarity, specificity, and scroll-stop, and shortlist the top 3 from at least 2 different formulas.

variations.label: Headline + full first-line pairing
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the headline needs to work together with the very next line (a subheadline, a first sentence), since a headline that's strong alone can fall flat if the next line doesn't follow through on it.
variations.prompt:
You are a headline specialist. The core message is: [ONE PLAIN SENTENCE — THE ACTUAL BENEFIT OR CLAIM]. Audience: [X]. Format: [e.g. blog title, email subject line, ad headline — specify length limit if relevant].

Generate 4 headline + first-line pairs, one for each of these formulas: benefit-led, curiosity-led, number-led (real numbers only: [PASTE ANY REAL FACTS/NUMBERS AVAILABLE]), problem-led. Each pair should show how the first line delivers on the headline's promise rather than restating it. Score each pair 1-5 on clarity, specificity, and whether the first line follows through.

variations.label: Competitor-aware headline set
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you already know what competitors' headlines tend to sound like and want yours to stand out from that pattern specifically, not just be generically different.
variations.prompt:
You are a headline specialist. The core message is: [ONE PLAIN SENTENCE — THE ACTUAL BENEFIT OR CLAIM]. Audience: [X]. Format: [e.g. blog title, email subject line, ad headline].

What competitor headlines in this space commonly sound like: [DESCRIBE OR PASTE 2-3 EXAMPLES]

Generate 12 headlines (3 each across benefit-led, curiosity-led, number-led using only real numbers: [PASTE ANY REAL FACTS/NUMBERS AVAILABLE], and direct-address) that deliberately avoid sounding like the competitor pattern described above. Score each 1-5 on clarity, specificity, scroll-stop, and how distinct it is from the competitor pattern.

followUps.label: Scores look inflated — sanity-check the top ones
followUps.prompt: Look again at the 3 highest-scoring headlines and tell me honestly if any of them are actually vague or generic despite the high score. Re-score them more critically if so.

followUps.label: One formula is weak — regenerate just that category
followUps.prompt: The [FORMULA NAME] headlines are the weakest of the five categories. Regenerate just those 4, pushing for something more specific and less generic than what's there now.

followUps.label: Check no stat was inflated or invented
followUps.prompt: Go through every number-led headline and confirm each figure matches exactly what I gave you in the real facts, with no rounding up or added claims.

followUps.label: Shortlist from different formulas than my instinct
followUps.prompt: Ignore my likely favorites for a second — based purely on the scores, give me the 3 headlines that scored highest across at least 3 different formulas, not just my top-scoring category.

copy-b3-headline-systems.walkthrough:
Grace is writing headline options for a budgeting app that, per the company's own product data, finds users an average of $200 a month in unused subscriptions.

She opens Claude and pastes the headline-systems prompt: core message is the $200/month stat, audience is people who suspect they're overpaying for subscriptions but haven't checked, format is a blog title with no strict length limit, and the real facts available are just the $200/month figure from the last 6 months of product data.

Claude returns 20 headlines across five formulas, each scored: benefit-led ("Find the $200 a month you didn't know you were losing"), curiosity-led ("The subscription costing you $200 a month, hiding in plain sight"), number-led using the real $200 figure rather than inventing a bigger one, direct-address ("You're probably paying for something you forgot about"), and problem-led ("Stop paying for subscriptions you don't use"). Each headline has clarity, specificity, and scroll-stop scores with a one-line reason.

Grace notices the curiosity-led category scored consistently lower than the others and reads a little vague. She sends the follow-up: "The curiosity-led headlines are the weakest category — regenerate just those 4, pushing for something more specific." Claude returns four sharper options, each now naming the specific subscription-tracking mechanic rather than staying abstract.

She does her own sanity check on the top 5 scored headlines, confirms the $200 figure appears correctly everywhere it's used, and shortlists three finalists spanning the benefit-led, number-led, and revised curiosity-led categories. Total time: about 12 minutes.

placeholders.name: LIST 2-4 SPECIFIC CLAIMS, e.g. "average time small businesses spend on invoicing per month," "industry adoption rate of X in 2025-2026," "typical cost difference between X and Y"
placeholders.what: The exact specific claims you want to make in your copy, named precisely — not a broad topic to research generally. A good claim is specific enough to actually be answered with one figure or fact; a bad one is a broad request like "tell me about this industry," which returns unfocused general information instead of a checkable claim.
examples: average time small businesses spend on manual invoicing per month; typical error rate in manually reconciled books
percentage of remote teams reporting meeting fatigue in 2025-2026; average number of status meetings per week for a mid-size team
average cost difference between hiring a part-time bookkeeper versus using bookkeeping software; typical time small business owners spend on bookkeeping weekly

placeholders.name: WHAT THE COPY IS FOR AND WHO IT'S FOR
placeholders.what: The context this research will feed into — what piece of copy you're writing and who it's for. This helps the model judge which facts are actually relevant and how to phrase the suggested copy line at the end.
examples: A landing page hero section for a small-business invoicing tool, aimed at solo freelancers and very small agencies.
A LinkedIn ad for a remote-work productivity tool, targeting mid-size company operations managers.
An email nurture sequence for bookkeeping software, aimed at small business owners currently doing their own books.

variations.label: Single high-stakes claim, deep verification
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you have one specific, important claim you plan to use prominently (a hero headline, a press release) and need thorough verification rather than a quick multi-claim sweep.
variations.prompt:
Research this single claim in depth and find the most current, authoritative source available. Do not state anything as fact without a source; say explicitly if you cannot find a reliable one.

Claim to research: [ONE SPECIFIC CLAIM]
Context: [WHAT THE COPY IS FOR AND WHO IT'S FOR]

Find: the specific fact/figure, the most authoritative source you can find (prioritize original research or primary sources over secondary articles citing them), publication date, and note if multiple sources disagree on the figure. Flag if the source is more than 2 years old. Then suggest 2 different ways to phrase this claim as a direct, specific copy line, each embedding the figure naturally.

variations.label: Competitor-comparison claims
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the claims you want to make are explicitly comparative (cheaper than, faster than, more X than) rather than standalone industry facts, which need extra care to avoid overstating.
variations.prompt:
Research the following comparative claims and find current, citable sources for each. Do not state a comparison as fact without a source for both sides of it; if you can't verify both sides, say so rather than guessing.

Comparative claims to research: [LIST 2-3 COMPARISONS, e.g. "our category's typical cost vs. hiring in-house," "time saved vs. manual process"]
Context: [WHAT THE COPY IS FOR AND WHO IT'S FOR]

For each, give: both figures being compared, sources and dates for each, and a note on whether the comparison is apples-to-apples or has caveats worth knowing before using it in copy. Then suggest one honest, specific copy line for each comparison.

variations.label: Ongoing fact-sheet builder for a recurring topic
variations.whenToUse: Use this to build (or refresh) a running reference document for a topic you write about often, rather than researching from scratch for a single piece.
variations.prompt:
I'm building a running fact sheet on [TOPIC] that I'll reuse across multiple pieces of copy over the next few months. Research current, citable facts on: [LIST 4-6 SUBTOPICS OR CLAIM AREAS]

For each: the specific fact/figure, source and URL, publication date, and a one-line note on how confident/authoritative the source is. Flag anything older than 2 years. Format this as a clean reference table I can save and re-check before reusing any fact in future copy, since some of these may go stale before I use them again.

followUps.label: Verify the source actually says this
followUps.prompt: For the claim about [SPECIFIC CLAIM], give me the direct source link so I can open it and confirm it actually supports the figure you gave me, worded the way you summarized it.

followUps.label: This stat is too old — find something more current
followUps.prompt: The source for [SPECIFIC CLAIM] is more than 2 years old. Search again specifically for something more recent, and if nothing more current exists, tell me clearly instead of reusing the old figure.

followUps.label: No good source — help me phrase it honestly
followUps.prompt: You couldn't find a solid source for [SPECIFIC CLAIM]. Suggest an honest, softer version of this claim that doesn't require a specific unverifiable number, while still being useful in the copy.

followUps.label: Turn the verified facts into copy
followUps.prompt: Using only the facts you found sources for, write [NUMBER] versions of a single sentence for [WHERE IT WILL APPEAR, e.g. "the hero subheadline"] that embeds the real figure directly and specifically, without vague phrasing like "studies show."

copy-i1-research-backed-copy.walkthrough:
Marcus writes copy for a bookkeeping software company and wants to open a new landing page with a specific, credible claim about how much time small businesses spend on manual bookkeeping — not a vague "studies show" line.

He opens ChatGPT, checks that Deep Research is available on his Plus plan, and selects it in the composer instead of a normal chat. He pastes the research prompt: claims to research are "average time small business owners spend on their own bookkeeping weekly" and "average cost of hiring a part-time bookkeeper," with context that this is for a landing page hero aimed at small business owners currently doing their own books. ChatGPT asks one quick clarifying question about which region to focus on; he answers "United States."

About ten minutes later, the report comes back: a figure for the weekly bookkeeping time with a named source and a 2025 date, flagged as current, and a cost figure for part-time bookkeepers with a separate source. It also suggests a copy line embedding the real hours figure directly.

Marcus opens the source for the time-spent figure himself to confirm the summary matches what the article actually says — it does, and the number is even more specific than he expected.

He wants to double-check the bookkeeper cost figure feels right for his specific market, so he sends the follow-up: "The source for the bookkeeper-cost claim — give me the direct link so I can confirm it supports the figure as summarized." ChatGPT provides the link, and Marcus finds it's from a regional survey that may run a bit high for his audience, so he decides to leave that specific number out and use the time-spent stat instead, which he trusts more.

He writes the verified time figure directly into his hero subheadline, noting the source and date in his working doc in case a client asks. Total time: about 20 minutes, including the wait for the report — he made sure to start it early rather than five minutes before he needed the copy.

placeholders.name: PASTE DRAFT
placeholders.what: The original draft that the client feedback applies to, pasted in full. Include everything, not just the sections you think got feedback — the model needs the whole piece to apply changes accurately and produce a usable change log.
examples: [Paste the full 250-word product email draft the client is reviewing]
[Paste the complete landing page hero and problem section, about 180 words]
[Paste the full 3-paragraph blog intro under review]

placeholders.name: PASTE ALL FEEDBACK
placeholders.what: All the client's feedback exactly as they gave it, even if it's messy, came from multiple emails, or is written casually — don't clean it up or summarize it before pasting. The model needs the raw, sometimes-contradictory feedback to correctly separate specific asks from vague direction and catch real contradictions.
examples: "Love the opening. Can we cut this down by half? Also make the CTA stronger. And can it feel a bit more premium — actually maybe keep it casual, our audience is pretty relaxed."
From Slack: "this is good but too long" — from email reply: "also can we lead with the discount instead of the feature? and drop the second paragraph entirely, feels redundant"

"Overall solid. A few things: 1) the second sentence is a bit awkward, 2) we should mention the free trial somewhere, 3) can it sound less like a template and more like us? not sure how to describe that exactly"

variations.label: Multiple stakeholders with conflicting feedback
variations.whenToUse: Use this when feedback came from more than one person on the client side and you need the contradictions clearly attributed to who said what, not just flagged generically.
variations.prompt:
You are revising the draft below based on feedback from multiple stakeholders. Separate the feedback into (a) specific asks and (b) vague/directional notes, and note which stakeholder gave which note. If any two stakeholders' notes contradict each other, list the contradiction explicitly with both names, rather than silently choosing one.

Original draft: [PASTE DRAFT]
Feedback from [STAKEHOLDER 1 NAME]: [PASTE]
Feedback from [STAKEHOLDER 2 NAME]: [PASTE]

Apply the specific asks first, exactly as stated, noting whose ask each was. Then address vague notes with concrete changes. End with a change log mapping each note (with stakeholder name) to the specific change made, and a clearly flagged list of any stakeholder contradictions that need a decision before this can be finalized.

variations.label: Second-round revision after partial feedback on round one
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a second (or later) round of revisions, where you need the new feedback applied on top of the already-revised draft, not the original.
variations.prompt:
You are applying a second round of client feedback to a draft that's already been revised once. Separate the feedback into (a) specific asks and (b) vague/directional notes before applying anything, and flag any contradiction with the round-one changes explicitly.

Current draft (after round 1): [PASTE CURRENT DRAFT]
Round 1 change log (for context, so you don't undo it accidentally): [PASTE ROUND 1 CHANGE LOG]
New client feedback (round 2): [PASTE ALL FEEDBACK]

Apply specific asks first, then vague notes with concrete named changes. End with a round-2 change log, and flag anywhere the new feedback seems to reverse a round-1 decision, rather than silently overwriting it.

variations.label: Feedback that includes a reference example
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the client's feedback includes a reference piece of writing ("more like this") rather than only verbal description, which is often a stronger signal than adjectives alone.
variations.prompt:
You are revising the draft below based on client feedback that includes a reference example of the tone/style they want. Separate the feedback into (a) specific asks and (b) vague/directional notes before applying anything.

Original draft: [PASTE DRAFT]
Client feedback: [PASTE ALL FEEDBACK]
Reference example the client pointed to as the tone/style they want: [PASTE REFERENCE EXAMPLE]

Apply the specific asks first, exactly as stated. Then use the reference example as a concrete pattern-match for any vague direction (like "more premium" or "punchier"), naming in the change log exactly what pattern from the reference you applied and where.

followUps.label: Double-check the change log against the original feedback
followUps.prompt: Go through the original feedback line by line and confirm each note is reflected somewhere in the change log. Flag anything from the feedback that doesn't appear to have been addressed.

followUps.label: This resolved a contradiction without asking — flag it properly
followUps.prompt: Looking at the notes about [DESCRIBE THE CONFLICTING FEEDBACK], you seem to have picked one interpretation without flagging it as a contradiction. Undo that choice and list it explicitly as a contradiction I need to resolve instead.

followUps.label: An unrequested change slipped in — revert it
followUps.prompt: The change to [SPECIFIC LINE OR SECTION] doesn't map to anything in the feedback I gave you. Revert that specific change back to the original draft's wording and leave everything else as is.

followUps.label: Translate a vague note more concretely
followUps.prompt: The change you made for the vague note "[VAGUE NOTE, e.g. more premium feel]" feels too subtle to actually register as a change. Make it more clearly, concretely different, and update the change log line to describe exactly what changed.

copy-i2-client-revision-rounds.walkthrough:
Elena is revising a product email for a client and receives feedback that's a little scattered: "Love the opening. Can we cut this down by half? Also make the CTA stronger. And can it feel a bit more premium — actually maybe keep it casual, our audience is pretty relaxed."

Rather than guessing at what the client really wants, she opens Claude and pastes the revision prompt with the full original draft and the feedback exactly as the client wrote it, unedited.

Claude separates the feedback: specific asks are "cut by half" and "stronger CTA"; it flags the contradiction between "more premium" and "keep it casual" explicitly rather than silently picking one. It applies the two specific asks first — shortening the draft and rewriting the CTA to be more direct — then notes that the tone request needs clarification before it can be applied. A change log lists each addressed item.

Elena reads the flagged contradiction and realizes the client probably meant something like "more polished, not more casual" rather than truly opposite requests, so she checks with the client directly and gets confirmation: they want it more polished but not stiff. She sends the follow-up: "Apply the tone request as 'more polished but not stiff' — the client confirmed that's what they meant, not literally casual and literally premium at the same time." Claude revises the copy accordingly and updates the change log entry.

She checks the final change log against the original feedback, confirms every note is addressed, and sends the revision back with the change log attached so the client can see exactly what moved. Total time: about 12 minutes, plus the quick clarifying question.

placeholders.name: PASTE 5-10 SAMPLES OF YOUR OWN BEST WRITING
placeholders.what: Real writing you've actually produced that you consider genuinely representative of your best, most distinctive work — not your average rushed output, and not writing you're unsure about. Pull from a few different formats (emails, headlines, longer pieces) if possible, since patterns that only show up in one format aren't fully your style, they're that format's convention.
examples: [Paste 3 of your best email openers, 2 headlines you're proud of, and one full short piece — like a blog intro or landing page section — you consider genuinely representative of how you write at your best]
[Paste 5 LinkedIn posts you wrote that got strong engagement and that you'd still stand behind today, plus 2 email subject lines you think are distinctly "you"]
[Paste your 4 favorite pieces of client work from the last year across different formats — an email, an ad headline set, a landing page paragraph, a social caption]

variations.label: Building a client or brand voice guide instead of your own
variations.whenToUse: Use this to build a reusable voice guide for a regular client or brand you write for, rather than your own personal voice — same mechanism, different subject.
variations.prompt:
Analyze the writing samples below and build a voice guide for [CLIENT/BRAND NAME]. Do not use vague adjectives alone (e.g. 'conversational,' 'punchy') — for every trait you name, identify the specific mechanism that creates it, with a quoted example from the samples.

Writing samples (their own past copy, not mine): [PASTE 5-10 SAMPLES OF THE CLIENT'S/BRAND'S BEST WRITING]

Produce a guide with: 1) sentence patterns (with quoted examples), 2) vocabulary habits — words favored and avoided, with examples, 3) structural habits, 4) 3-5 signature moves with quoted examples, 5) a paste-ready instruction block under 100 words for writing in this voice, built only from the patterns above.

variations.label: Quick version from fewer samples
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you don't have 5-10 strong samples handy and want a lighter first pass you can refine later as you gather more writing.
variations.prompt:
Analyze the writing samples below and build a short, first-pass style guide — treat this as a draft I'll refine once I have more samples. Do not use vague adjectives alone; for every trait you name, identify the specific mechanism with a quoted example.

Writing samples (fewer than ideal, working with what I have): [PASTE 2-4 SAMPLES]

Produce: 1) 2-3 sentence patterns you can identify even from this small sample, 2) any vocabulary habits you notice, 3) a short paste-ready instruction block (under 80 words), clearly flagged as a first draft to refine, noting which sections feel under-supported by too few examples.

variations.label: Compare your voice against a target voice you're trying to shift toward
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're deliberately trying to evolve your voice (e.g. sound less formal) rather than just capture what it already is — it produces a gap analysis instead of a pure description.
variations.prompt:
Analyze both sets of writing samples below. First, build a short style guide of my current voice from set A. Then compare it against set B (a voice I'm trying to move toward) and identify the 3-5 most specific, actionable differences — not vague ('be more casual') but mechanical ('set B uses contractions in nearly every sentence; set A rarely does').

My current writing (set A): [PASTE 4-5 SAMPLES]
Target voice I want to move toward (set B): [PASTE 4-5 SAMPLES]

End with a paste-ready instruction block (under 100 words) describing how to write like set B while still sounding like a more casual evolution of set A, not a completely different person.

followUps.label: Too vague — push for the actual mechanism
followUps.prompt: The trait "[VAGUE TRAIT, e.g. conversational]" still isn't concrete enough. Tell me exactly what mechanism creates that impression — sentence length, punctuation, word choice, structure — with a quoted example from my samples.

followUps.label: Test the instruction block on a new piece
followUps.prompt: Using only the paste-ready instruction block from the guide above, write [NEW PIECE, e.g. a LinkedIn post about X]. Don't reference the original samples directly — just the instruction block, the way I'd actually use it in a future prompt.

followUps.label: Instruction block is too long — tighten it
followUps.prompt: The paste-ready instruction block is longer than I want to paste into every prompt. Cut it to under 60 words while keeping the 2-3 most distinctive, load-bearing patterns.

followUps.label: This missed a pattern I know is really me
followUps.prompt: I think there's a pattern in my writing you missed: [DESCRIBE IT, e.g. "I almost always end paragraphs with a short one-line sentence"]. Check the samples for this pattern, and if it's really there, add it to the guide with a quoted example.

copy-a1-personal-style-guide-asset.walkthrough:
Theo has been freelance copywriting for two years and notices AI drafts never quite sound like him — they're competent but generic. He decides to build a real style guide instead of continuing to describe his voice from memory each time.

He gathers eight samples of writing he's genuinely proud of: three email openers, two headlines, and three short passages from past landing pages and blog intros — deliberately picking his best work, not average output.

In Claude, he pastes the style-guide prompt with all eight samples. Claude returns a structured guide: sentence patterns (a habit of opening with a 4-8 word declarative sentence followed by one longer explanatory sentence, with two quoted examples), vocabulary habits (a near-total avoidance of the word "leverage" and a preference for concrete verbs over adjectives), structural habits, and 3-5 signature moves each with a quoted example — plus a paste-ready 85-word instruction block summarizing it all.

To test it, Theo sends the follow-up: "Using only the instruction block, write a LinkedIn post about time management for freelancers — don't reference the original samples directly." The resulting post opens with a short declarative sentence and avoids the vocabulary the guide flagged, and it genuinely reads like something he'd write.

He shows the test post to a colleague without telling her it was AI-assisted, and she doesn't flag anything as off. Satisfied, he saves the instruction block in a notes app for quick pasting into future prompts. Total time: about 20 minutes.
